utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will let the Chamber know in due course whether there's any prospect of calling the last witness that we've been considering. I think we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Wait for the witness for one moment, please. Before Mr. Saxon calls the next witness, there are a couple of administrative things I would like to deal with. First, as the Chamber will no doubt have noted, in his cross-examination yesterday, it's now clear that the defendant was using materials, in particular the interview of Dr. Rugova that had been served on him by the Prosecution, and I can inform the Chamber they were served on him as long ago as January of this year. So he's now making use of and having access to those materials. But it's more important that I remind the Chamber that there were three press articles concerning Dr. Rugova that the Chamber thought it prudent to lay before you, notwithstanding the fact that they haven't been formally dealt with by the accused in cross-examination. Now, those three press articles were three of 39 press articles that were served on him in January. They weren't served as exculpatory under 68. They were served at that time -- he referred to three or four out of 39. They weren't served under 68. They were served at a time when an approach was taken to public material and our obligation to serve public material, which is not a position we currently hold. So he was served more material than it was our duty to serve and that we would currently serve. However, he got the 39 press articles. It may be thought fairer simply to provide the Chamber not just with the four, three or four, but with all 39, because no doubt there was a selection made. We're in the Chamber's hands. We can produce just the four or we can produce all 39 which were the relevant press interviews of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be sensible to produce the four rather than produce more paper; for you to have a look at it and see if there are any other articles that you would have produced in re-examination if the witness had been asked about those four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That seems very sensible. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then we would -- we will take the bundle when you've got that ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. We'll deal with that. The second matter is a couple of additional exhibits that were wanted. There's the constitution of Kosovo which we now have copied. Can that be distributed. I think a number may have already been allocated to it, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure this has been exhibited. We've had the constitution of the FRY, and I think we've had the constitution of Serbia, but I don't think we've had the constitution --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, we certainly haven't. It may be we had allocated a number to it because I know His Honour Judge Robinson wanted it yesterday and I said I'd produce it, but if not --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours' this will be Prosecutor's Exhibit number 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the accused, I think, was raising the absence of a Serbian version of the education agreement, Exhibit 127. We have now managed to locate a Cyrillic Serbian version of that agreement. May that go as part of 127 rather than have its own number? Your Honour, that's all I desire to raise at the moment, save simply to remind the Chamber that if K4 is available on Thursday, the question of 92 bis statements processed here will then fall for determination with that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is no constitution. It says here Kacanik and Pristina. That is an illegal document brought in by a group of Albanian separatists who could not have had any legal effective value in the system of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard the evidence about it, and it was admitted because it was asked for, but we know what was said about it. Now, can we have a witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Fadil Vishi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should say that before he comes in, we will return the last -- the papers we had in relation to the last witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just ask, before the witness walks in? You mentioned a new list of witnesses dated the 2nd or 3rd of May, and the last one I have is dated the 29th of April, and it was my understanding that we would have programmes for at least one week, and now I see that they are changing it yet again. Can we establish the following kind of practice; that we at least know for one week what the witnesses will be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the -- that should be the practice and is. Occasionally, inevitably, there have to be changes, but they're to be kept to a minimum. Perhaps the Prosecution could see that there is this document of the 2nd of May, if it hasn't been, is served on the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that as soon as we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Fadil Vishi?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, were you born on the 1st of November, 1961?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Dubrava in the municipality of Kacanik in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is the village of Dubrava about eight or nine kilometres to the north-west of the town of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, in October of 1999, did you give a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor regarding the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo earlier in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 30th of January of this year, in the village of Dubrava in the municipality of Kacanik, were you provided with a copy of the statement that you made in October of 1999 in the presence of representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time, did you attest that the copy provided to you was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Subsequently, during discussions with members of the Office of the Prosecutor, did you indicate that there is an error in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you the paragraph where that error occurs. It's on page 4, the fifth paragraph of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the benefit of the accused, I believe it's on the top of the last page of the Serbian version. There is a paragraph that says the following: "From the convoy, the soldiers arrested six persons. The others went to Macedonia. Two of these six persons were released a short time after, but the four were sent to Ferizaj, where they were tortured in the police station."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Should that sentence actually end with the words, "tortured in the coffee bar called Pranvera," rather than "police station"?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that correction made on the record, I would now offer that statement into evidence under Rule 92 bis. And I will also, once you have a copy of the statement, I will point out to you where the correction should be made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit number 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The correction that we just made was on page 4 of the English version, in the middle of the page, the fifth paragraph starting from the top, in the very last sentence. Rather than saying, "police station," it should say, "the coffee bar called Pranvera." And in the Albanian version, it is on page 6, in the middle of the page. Your Honours, Fadil Vishi is a Kosovo Albanian Muslim from the village of Dubrava in the municipality of Kacanik. From about the New Year of 1999, according to his statement, the village of Dubrava was more or less isolated. The population was not allowed to leave the village, and the telephone and electricity was cut off. After awhile, basic supplies became limited, and the villagers were forced to smuggle necessities during the night. On the 25th of May, 1999, Serbian forces surrounded the village of Dubrava. The witness woke up his neighbours, and they all gathered by the village school. Mr. Vishi fled and watched what happened in the village from the woods above. Most of the population left on tractors and trailers and started to drive towards Macedonia. After awhile, the convoy was stopped and six men were arrested. In the evening, the witness could see that his house was burning. Rrahim Vishi and Milaim Vishi were found killed close to the witness's home. About 50 metres from the witnesses home Ali and Xhemail Tusha were found killed. On the following day, 26 May, 1999, in addition, the villagers found the bodies of Hajrush Qorri and his son and daughter. They also found the body of Rexhep Qorri. The body of Sylejman Gurri, who had been captured by VJ soldiers several weeks earlier, was found in the woods about two kilometres from the village. The witness remained in the forest until the following day and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then walked 24 hours to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement given on the 18th of October, 1999, you say literally -- this is on page 1 of the statement, I'm going to quote it: "We lost every freedom. We totally lost our freedom. From last New Year, we were not allowed to leave the Dubrava area. The Serbs took out, cut off the electricity and the telephone and we had no possibility to get information from the outside world. We didn't know anything about what was going on in Kosovo before the KFOR troops came in June 1999." Are these your words? Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Very true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they did not allow you to leave Dubrava from the last New Year, do you mean from the 1st of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is to say that none of the Albanians from the village - it was a purely Albanian village, right? - could not leave Dubrava all that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how was it that the Serbs prevented you from leaving the area of Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: They didn't want us to leave the village because -- we didn't want to leave the village because it was our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not want to leave the village. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that it was the Serbs who prevented you from leaving the Dubrava area. So what is correct; did the Serbs prevent you from leaving the Dubrava area or was it you who did not want to leave the Dubrava area?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Even if we'd wanted to leave, we didn't have anywhere to go because the entire village was encircled on all sides by military forces, by Serbian military and police forces. And that's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you that you were not allowed to leave the Dubrava area?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: We had no kind of contact with the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you see them, then, when you didn't have any kind of contact?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: We understood that the Serbian forces were somewhere one kilometre from us, and they were stationed at the factory in Silkapor, and they moved on the road that leads to the border and to Skopje and, on the other side, on the road to Tetovo. And there were forces positioned in what are called the Sharr mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that the forces were facing the border with Macedonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: They had nothing to face up to on the border because nothing happened on the border. They were aimed against the populous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you spent all of two months, as you had put it, in their immediate vicinity, and they didn't do anything to you. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: It's not quite like that, because several times we were maltreated. They provoked us in various ways. And on the 12th of March, they shelled from the Silkapor factory, aiming at our village and at a part of the woods where they damaged the house of an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how was it that they maltreated you, when you said only a minute ago that you did not have any contact with them whatsoever for all of two months?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I repeat, we didn't have any contact, but they communicated with us in their own way, and they had their own way of doing things, and with their military vehicles and their equipment. They did what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is not clear to me. You did not have any contact. That means that you didn't have any contact with them, and they didn't have any contact with you. So then how did they communicate with you in their own special way?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I didn't say that we communicated, but we were surrounded by Serbian forces, and we didn't dare leave the village. But they shelled us, shelled our village on the 12th of March, and a stretch of the woods where there were some houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for this shelling on the 12th of March, why did you say nothing about it in your statement? You mentioned that something happened on the 25th of May but not in March.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: In my statement, I spoke specifically about the kidnapping of various people that was committed by your forces, the kidnapping of three people. These forces kidnapped three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Please. First you say that you had no contact during the first two months, and now -- that is to say, from the New Year onwards, as you had put it, from the 1st of January, 1999. And now you are introducing yet a new piece of information, that you were shelled by them on the 12th of March. Please think about this. What is the truth out of the two? Because both cannot be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is -- that is not a fair comment. The comment which you make is that they -- there is nothing in the statement about the shelling of the 12th of March, and the witness said, in answer to that, that he spoke specifically about the kidnapping of various people and that that was what his statement was concerned with. So to say there's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon? But now during the examination-in-chief, he says things that were not dealt with in his statement, and he certainly would have had to have included that in the statement had this actually have happened. So that should be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why -- Mr. Vishi, since the point is made, why did you not include this incident of the 12th of March in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought of including only the part of my statement which was related to kidnapping and the offensive in which these were killed, while there were -- there are other witnesses who can testify to everything else that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you thought that you should include only the part of your statement that was related to kidnapping, does that mean that you had given a broader statement and that this particular statement is only a part of that longer statement?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: My statement, which is in front of us, is mostly about the kidnapping and the killing of these people and the course of the offensive against the village on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that your comprehensive statement then, not only a part of it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't understand what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To put it more simply: Did you make any other statement, or is this the only one that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement which I've prepared for you here is about the kidnapping and the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is: Did you make any other statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When was it that Serbs, as you had put it, cut off your electricity and all communications?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1999, we were without all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So from that moment, from the beginning of 1999 until June, your village had no electricity; right? And there were no exceptions to that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is your claim that the soldiers from the Sharr mountains were deployed in such a way that they were able to see every little move that you'd make?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far away were they from you? They were on Sharr, on the mountain of Sharr. So how far away was that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: The truth is that we didn't go deep into the mountains. It was -- it was only about four kilometres away where they were positioned. Every day they passed in front of the village, between two roads that lead to Skopje and Tetovo, and were able to see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say every move that you'd make, are you referring to the villagers, to all the inhabitants of that village when you say "you"?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the army and the police that you led.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what you said, that from there they could see every move you'd make, you. Every move you would make. When you say every move that you would make, is the "you" the villagers?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serbian military and police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct what you said, that from these positions, they could stop anyone who would be coming to that area and leaving it? Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I said that from that time, we never moved from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that they could stop everyone, anyone who would want to leave the village or come into the village. That was your assertion.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: If we had gone out, that's the sort of thing they would have done, from my experience of other places. But we didn't go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you mean that from a four-kilometre distance, as you had put it - you say that that's how far away they were from you - that they could stop anyone who would want to come into the village or get out of the village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I said the distance where they were positioned was four kilometres away, but their movements brought us -- brought them closer than a hundred metres along the roads going to Skopje and Tetovo and from the factory at Silkapor, which is -- which is not more than one kilometre away, as the crow flies, from our village. The army was positioned with tanks all this time, pointing towards our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you claim that after the New Year, due to a shortage of supplies, the villagers started going out during the night, going shopping, and smuggling goods. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: The goods were brought by various people. And when these goods were brought, there were unfortunate incidents such as the kidnapping of three persons on the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, how is it possible that people go out shopping, that they come back to the village and all the rest you've said, when you say before that that the Serbs prevented you from moving outside the village or coming back into the village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I said before that we didn't leave the village, but -- but these things like groceries were brought by somebody called Ramadan Lami, who later, with his son, was kidnapped from his own home. And Ramadan Lami's body was found near the Silkapor factory. It was totally decomposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you just concentrate on the questions, and we'll get on more quickly. The point -- the point that was being made is if it was right that the Serb forces had surrounded the village so that people couldn't get in and out, how was it possible for these goods, these groceries, to be brought in? That's the question. Perhaps you can help us as to that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is quite true. The person who brought these groceries lived in a village outside Dubrava called Kacanik i Vjeter where there were Serbian families also living, but under what agreement he was able to work, we don't know. Finally, he himself was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you used the word "smuggling"; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: We don't know how he brought these things, but he did bring these things. How he did it, only he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you used the word "smuggling" in your statement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: This is a kind of trade which he was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But did you use the word "smuggling" in your statement when speaking about him because that's what he was involved in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of his statement. Just a moment, Mr. Vishi. We'll have a copy of the statement and you can see it. Have you got it? He's got one. Well, Mr. Vishi, have a look at the first page, and in the English, seven paragraphs -- the seventh paragraph. It says: "The situation for food and other needed goods got worse after New Year, and the local people started smuggling goods into the villages from the outside." Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I think -- what I think you're being asked is: What did you mean by "smuggling" in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in the sense that in some cases -- that mainly groceries were brought by the above-mentioned person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But why did you call it smuggling? What else did he bring in, apart from the groceries? You said foodstuffs and other goods. What were the "other goods"?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I didn't call it contraband, but I said that he went in for trade. He brought these things, and he sold them in the village, because he didn't belong to our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But according to what you wrote in your statement, does that mean that this man, Ramadan Lami, was a smuggler, in fact?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I can't say that he went in for contraband, because in the end, he himself suffered badly, suffered the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about an attack on the village after which, as you say, the disintegrated body of Ramadan Lami was found by the villagers. Decomposed body. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That's right. His body was found after the offensive against the village of Dubrava on 25th of May. Several friends of mine found his body and took it away and buried him in his own village of Kacanik i Vjeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many days later was the body found after the attack on Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: His body was found three or four days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that before that attack, the attack that you're talking about, that he died before the attack?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That's right, because Ramadan Lami, after 5th of May, when the Serbian military and police forces kidnapped three people, he no longer came to our village. His -- only his body was found after 25th of May. Nobody can know when exactly he was killed except for your forces under your leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what makes you assume that he was killed by our forces?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, could he perhaps have been killed by somebody who wanted to loot him because he was a smuggler? Was there that possibility too, that somebody wanted to steal the goods from him?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I don't think so, because no Albanian could penetrate there because, as I said, military forces had been deployed there for quite a long time. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he wasn't found dead where the soldiers were deployed. He was found elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: He was not found elsewhere. He was found near the Silkapor factory, exactly where the soldiers were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "near"? How near?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: He was exactly in the place where the forces were positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that you assume that our forces had killed him and left his body to decompose there for several weeks in that place where it was found; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And who attacked your village and when?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Our village was attacked on the 25th of May, at about 3.30 in the morning. The village was attacked by Serb military and police forces. From all sides, the village was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The village was cut off from all sides, you say. And who did the Serbs attack from all sides in your village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: As I said, at about 3.30 in the morning, we had some guards, local people who were unarmed, who were keeping vigil of the village. They informed us that the village was encircled. And right away, and me personally, along with some other friends, we informed our co-villagers of the fact that we were encircled. We came to the -- we agreed that the villagers should meet in some place, gather there and see what we could do to go over to Macedonia out of fear that something else occurred in other places where the whole population was massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you then started along the road to Macedonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Not me personally, but people got on tractors, trailers, whatever they had, men, women, and children, and set out. We stopped for awhile on the road, and then they were ordered that persons from 18 to 60 should stay behind in the village. And then the convoy was allowed to continue. But after another kilometre of journey --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that later on. That's not what I was asking you now. But let's go back to the events of, as you say, the 5th of May. On that evening, you set off towards the main road to buy some cigarettes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't go to the main road, but I went near Lepence river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To buy some cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I went to the house of someone called Ramush Dogani, to ask him to bring me some cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What time was that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: It was around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the evening or in the morning?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: In the morning. In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were you coming from?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I was coming from my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as I've just understood you, you didn't go to buy the cigarettes from Lami but from Ramush Dogani; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Ramush Dogani to ask him that when Lami comes with his goods, he should set aside for me these cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you reserved two kilogrammes of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: It is wrong, because I wanted to say two stacks of cigarettes, cartons of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here two kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: It may be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, your statement was read back to you, and you were asked a moment ago by the Prosecutor whether everything that is said in the statement is correct, and you didn't indicate that that was a mistake of any kind.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I don't consider it any big mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it were two kilogrammes, I would have to ask you who you needed two kilogrammes of cigarettes for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he says it was two cartons. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who is Sylejman Gurri?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Sylejman Gurri is the son-in-law of a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is he from Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: He's not from Dubrava. He's from Nik village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did Sylejman Gurri do?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Sylejman Gurri, he was a sick person. He didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said he was together with two people whom you didn't know. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those two people weren't from Dubrava; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No, they weren't from Dubrava. They were from Biqefc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From which village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Biqefc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were two men, is that right, two males?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: They were two young men, my age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw three people wearing uniforms arresting Sylejman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you saw with your own eyes; is that right? You saw him actually being arrested?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody else see that take place?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: There were two other persons who were with me who saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are their names?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I said earlier I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to what we were saying. You set out on the 25th of May, when the soldiers, as you say, encircled the village, surrounded the village, and you said that you personally woke up everybody in the neighbourhood and told them to get their tractors and set out for the Macedonian border; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they listen to you? Did they do what you said?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of authority did you have among those people for them to adhere to what you said straight away?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I was the leader of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were the leader of the village, the elder; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you help the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: We have supported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you tell the people to leave the village and go to Macedonia? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: We told them first to get together at the school of the village and then, after talking this thing over all together, they all agreed that the best choice for us - for them - would be to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And why weren't you in the convoy but, as you say, with a friend you were watching from the woods from a considerable height and seeing what was going on?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes. But if I were -- if I were part of the convoy, I wouldn't be here today to testify to what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And which six people from the convoy were arrested by the police? Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that two were let go, and the four others were taken away, and according to the correction you made, to the coffee bar. First of all you said to the police station, and then you said that it was in fact the coffee bar. So why would the police take them off to the coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Two persons were let go after awhile because they were of a young age, whereas the others, they didn't let them go. And they took them to Ferizaj, to a cellar of a coffee bar, where they maltreated them in most various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Then on 29th of May, they released them from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they released them four days later. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, after a lot of maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who did you stay in the forests with?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I was with a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that on that day, in the evening, as you said, you noticed that your house was on fire. Is that right, that that's when you noticed this?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that the people who tried to put out the fire -- so this was on the 26th of May, was it, is that right? -- that you noticed the bodies of Muharrem and Rrahim Vishi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Milaim Vishi and Rrahim Vishi are their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come they were in your yard?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: On the 25th of May -- excuse me. On the 5th of May, half an hour before Sylejman Gurri was kidnapped, these two persons were also kidnapped, as many eyewitnesses said. And up to the 25th of May, nobody knew anything of their whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's precisely why I'm asking you, because that's what it says in your statement. In your yard, on the 26th of May, when you say they disappeared on the 5th of May. So for a full 20 days. And then 20 days later, they appeared, dead, in your yard.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they disappeared on the 5th and turned up on the 25th in your yard, dead; right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of the KLA in your place at all?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the headquarters of the so-called 162nd Kacanik Brigade were located in your village? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: That is not true. The headquarters was stationed, the army existed, but not there in the mountains, a long way from the village. And it was not in that territory that belonged to Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far from the village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So nearer than the army was. The army, you said, was at four kilometres distance. Now, the two men that you said disappeared on the 5th of May, did they go to join them on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: This happened in other place -- in the other place of the village. The men who were kidnapped were kidnapped on the road that leads to Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Where your army was situated in the western part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. That's clear. Now, Ibush Vishi from Dubrava, is he a cousin of yours?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know Ahmet and Agim Vishi, also from Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Ibush Vishi the commander of the brigade and Ahmet his deputy? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Ibush Vishi, during that time, was not there; he was in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you where he was at that time, but was he the commander of that brigade and Ahmet his deputy? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about Agim? Was he a member of the so-called Hochstab of the 62nd Brigade? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the 25th of May, when the convoy was set up, did you transfer an order by someone to the people to leave the village? Yes or no. Were you conveying an order?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No. We received orders from no one. But we did that because of fear. Knowing what had happened in other villages, the population decided to flee the country, the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's sufficiently clear. I don't want to lose any more time, waste any more time with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have only two matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Witness, you say that you supported the KLA. In which way? What support did you provide?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I supported the KLA morally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And on top of that, also materially?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from the KLA, as village leader?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you pass any information to the KLA in your role as village leader? For example, on the arrival of Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Only after the population left to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. The other thing I want to clarify is you adjusted your statement by saying that out of these six persons that were arrested, four of them were sent to Ferizaj where they were tortured in a coffee bar. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: We know because I saw them when they were separated from the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand that. But were you present at the coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, one question: Could you clarify the meaning of what you said in your statement? Could you look at your statement. It's in the fourth paragraph of the first page. "We totally lost our freedom. From last New Year, we are not allowed to leave the Dubrava area." Have you found it? "... we are not allowed to leave the Dubrava area." In the Albanian language, it seems to be the third sentence of the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you hear from Serb forces not to leave the village in a specific language? What do you mean by you are not allowed to leave the village? They ordered you to stay in the village? What's the meaning of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't order us because we didn't have contact with them, but we didn't dare leave the village out of fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, a moment ago Mr. Wladimiroff asked you whether you were present in the coffee bar when the four men from your village were held there, and your answer was no. You said, on cross-examination, that these men were released on the 29th of May. Following their release on the 29th of May, did you have occasion to speak with one or more of these men who had been held in the coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall the name or names of these men?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: One was Emrush Dullovi. There was Naser Gurri. There was Nebi Hajdari, and there was Isuf Malsiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what did these men tell you about the treatment they had received when they were held in coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: They told me that they were mistreated in the harshest way. They were beaten to the extent, and electricity was used on them. And they said that they laid all that time in the blood of the people who had been in that cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did these men tell you who had mistreated them?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: They didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's go back to the 5th of May. You described in your cross-examination how you saw three men wearing uniforms arresting, as you put it, Sylejman Gurri. Were you able to recognise the uniforms worn by these three men?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: We saw their uniforms. They were camouflage uniforms. They didn't have caps. They had automatic rifles in their hands. One of them was tall, thin, pale, and light-coloured fair and face, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you at that time associate the uniforms worn by those men with a particular force?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I only saw them for a moment, and we merely saw that they were military uniforms, camouflage uniforms, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you hear if these men who were arresting Sylejman Gurri said anything to Sylejman Gurri?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: On the moment when they came out into the road where they were stationed, they jumped up from three different places and ordered Sylejman Gurri to stop and to put his hands up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What language did these three men in uniform speak at that time?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: They spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to change the subject now. On cross-examination, you were asked some questions about the attack on your village on the 25th of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. May, and the accused asked you who did the Serbs attack in your village, and I'd like to explore that theme a little bit with you. Following the attack on your village, to your knowledge was any video made of any persons killed on the 25th of May in Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When was that video made?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: On the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who was that video made by?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: It was made by a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is the name of your cousin who made that video?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: Fahri Vishi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And subsequently, has Fahri Vishi given that videotape to you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL VISHI
utterances.text: I asked him to give me this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a copy of this video and it's with the members of the audio-visual department, and I would like to play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, how does it arise from cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The accused asked this witness who the Serbs attacked, and on this video, we will see the bodies of some of the people who died in that attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not going to admit it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vishi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. May, may I ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got this list of witnesses dated the 2nd of May. It doesn't differ in any way from the list dated 29th of April. However, we heard a short while ago that they want to call Witness K4 the day after tomorrow, and that date had been fixed for the 15th of May. I assume that when we have three or four witnesses a day, it is quite clear that I cannot read 10 or 15 witnesses in advance because that is totally impossible. Therefore, I think that particularly these fixed witnesses should not be changed, that they should not make these changes at such short notice and calling them in advance. According to this list dated the 29th of April, he was planned for the 15th of May. And these are fixed witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will take this up with the Prosecution in due course because this isn't the only case of this change. Yes. Perhaps, Ms. Romano, you could pass that on to Mr. Nice, that we would like to discuss with him, if he can come tomorrow sometime, this business of the changes of the timetabling.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that Mr. Nice will come at the end of the session for other matters also, and he will be able to address this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Florim Krasniqi. Your Honours, in order to help with the testimony, the witness will testify about the area of Urosevac, and particularly the city of Mirosavlje. And this is the Kosovo atlas, page 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, please, can you state your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Florim Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: 7th of November, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And where do you live?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In Mirosale village of Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you were interviewed on the 23th of April, 1999, by members of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I remember it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, did you give a statement to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And on the 1st of February of this year, 2002, you appeared before a presiding officer appointed by the Registry of this Tribunal. Do you remember that as well?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity to review your statement, and you were given a copy of your statement in the Albanian language; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You also gave additional information that is comprised in an addendum; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to submit the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit number 138.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The summary of the witness's testimony is the following: The witness is an Albanian male from the village of Mirosavlje in the municipality of Urosevac. On 4th of April, the witness saw military vehicles on the road from Gnjilane to Urosevac positioned near the village of Softovic. They shelled towards the villages of Rahovica and Zlatare, killing four people in Zlatare and wounding another five people. The next day, the witness heard shelling, firing, and tanks moving in the direction of Pojatiste, following which about 1.000 internally displaced persons from surrounding villages arrived in Mirosavlje. One of these displaced persons was from Pojatiste and told the witness that Serb forces had shot a number of people in his village. The witness attended the funerals of these men and has prepared a hand-drawn map showing the area between Mirosavlje and Pojatiste and indicating four gravesites where the dead were buried, which is attached to his statement. On 7 April 1999, the witness saw houses burning in Sojevo and Kamena Glava in the municipality of Urosevac. He later heard that seven people died in Sojevo, having been shot. On 8th of April, 1999, Serb military vehicles came to his village. As soon as the vehicles were at the outskirts of the village, the soldiers jumped out and ran towards the houses. The witness and his family headed to the centre of their village. They joined other villagers and displaced persons who were fleeing, numbering hundreds. En route, the convoy was harassed and insulted by Serb forces, and the witness saw many burned houses and destroyed cars. The convoy was directed to Skopje by Serb police, but the witness stayed in Urosevac until 14 of April, 1999. On that date, the witness decided to leave Urosevac because every day he was hearing about killings and massacres by the Serbian army, and he felt it was too dangerous to stay. The witness then boarded a bus to Djeneral Jankovic, and at the border, police entered the bus and checked identification papers. The bus continued to the train station, where the police separated the people and collected money from the heads of the families. They were ordered to walk down the middle of the railway track to Macedonia. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard here now about killings, shootings, woundings, et cetera, but my question is going to be very precise. Did you personally see any one of these events that you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I didn't see their execution, but I buried the victims myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you had seen a single one of these events. Is the answer yes or no? You personally.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't see the events myself, but I saw the casualties. I buried the bodies that were killed -- of the people who were killed by your soldiers, and I saw how the bodies were totally deformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you see this alleged execution in Pojatiste? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Pojatishte cannot be -- is not visible from my village because of the high hills, but the volleys of automatic rifle fire, when these victims were executed, were audible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim that one of the victims of this alleged execution that you had not seen was a certain Haxhi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right. I can confirm his name here and now. He was also called Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Further on, on page 3, in paragraph 3 of this statement, when you identify this Haxhi, you say his last name is Godeni; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you're not from Pojatiste.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's true. I'm not from Pojatishte. I'm from the village of Mirosale. However, he was from Ferizaj, and he had left Ferizaj and was temporarily staying in Pojatishte. When the Serbian forces entered Pojatishte, he was captured, and at the same time he was executed alongside villagers from Pojatishte.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is what you had not seen, but that is what you claim. You also claim that, according to this alleged execution that you've been speaking about, there was a victim whose name you did not know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The victim whose name I did not then know was called Bajram Godeni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, allegedly he's from the village of Smira. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Somebody else is from the village of Smira. This is somebody who survived death but received very serious wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement you say that you saw him later, this man, this man who had been executed, that you saw him later and that his name is Shaban, but you don't know his last name. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right. His name is Shaban.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see him? Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't see Shaban. I saw Hasim. But it seems you haven't read the statement as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did this man who you saw say to you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Hasim? This man I met is Hasim, who told me in detail about the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was he also executed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He too --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- stick to the facts. Yes. What did he tell you, this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This man said that Serbian soldiers had gathered six people together, including Hasim. Hasim, together with them, was taken -- were taken by a soldier and escorted to a place on the edge of the village. There suddenly, when they arrived there, they forced them -- and they surrounded them, and one of them fired an automatic weapon. And of these people, three died on the spot, two were wounded, and Hasim escaped, merely catching a bullet on his jacket, on the sleeve of his coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did these people shoot at them or above their heads?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The soldier fired at them, and so the -- where the bullet landed decided the fate of the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Hasim escaped when he saw that they would shoot; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could he see then whether three men were killed, two wounded, et cetera, when he was fleeing from those who were shooting and who could not hit him?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Hasim didn't say how many victims got killed. He only said that they were shot at. But he knew nothing about the fate of the others. It was only later that we found out who the victims were, who the injured and the dead were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you find that out from?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We found that out because the son of Osman Mehmeti and Shaban's son, Muharrem, went near that place after Hasim told them where that shooting place was, and in the -- they were in danger of their lives because the shooting still continued when they went closer to the place, and they crawled near to that place and pulled the bodies away, the injured, who was Osman, while the old man, Shaban, though injured, had left, because they were not lethal injuries for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of injuries did they have, this man who left the execution site himself and the one that was wounded? What kind of injuries did they have?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From what we heard from the nurse who administered the first aid, Osman had injuries on his belly and on his leg. A bullet had entered his leg and, as a result of it, he had received an injury. And because of the bloodshed, he died at 1.00 in the morning, because of lack of medical assistance right away. His son who was also injured, he was lucky because the bullet hit him in the watch that was in his pocket so that deviated the trajectory of the bullet. He was received in the leg too [as interpreted], but he was slightly injured, so he was able to escape death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So some fled, some were executed, some were hit in the arm, some in the leg. Is that what you've been trying to explain?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Which nurse can give full details about these men? Please give her name and the address where she lives at now.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That nurse is called Nerxhivane Berisha from Mirosale village, and to this day she lives there. She has finished the high medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far away is the village of Sojevo from your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Sojevo village is about four to five kilometres away from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many Albanian families lived in Sojevo?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure of all the Albanian families living there because it's up to them to know the locals there. I know that it is a village inhabited mainly by Kosovars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But how many live there, approximately? I'm not asking for the accurate figure anyway.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: An approximate figure, since the neighbourhoods are situated far from each other, I might say that it has about 200 households.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two hundred households?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Between 150 to 200. Up to 200, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How many citizens does that make altogether, to the best -- to your best estimate?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have not counted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many members does an average household in Sojevo have?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: This is a ridiculous question, I would say, because I haven't visited each and every one of the households of Sojevo to count their members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you see seven people killed in Sojevo?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I heard about it from eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that it is true that these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know because people came from Sojevo to Mirosale and back and forth, and those people -- it was easy to bring them from Sojevo to my village at Mirosale because it is a mountainous area. And they have confirmed to us that they were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How were they killed?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They were executed by your army. Among them, there were some victims whose bodies were carbonised later on, completely charred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this village which has 200 households, approximately, that is to say a population of about 2.000, somebody went off and killed seven of the inhabitants there, according to what they told you?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At the beginning, we were told that only seven persons were killed, but after the war, we found out that there were more. Actually, their number was over -- more than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you claim that on the 7th of April, you saw some fires. Is that right? Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it seemed to you that it was houses in Sojevo and Kamena Glava that were on fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw it because my house is situated on a higher ground, and from there, I have a very good position to see what was going on. In this case, in the Sojevo village, I could see the burning houses, and Kamena Glava village. I saw the smoke rising in the sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whose houses burned down in Sojevo? Do you know the names of these persons?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw the burning houses. For the moment, it didn't matter whose house that was or those were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you whether you know whose houses had burned down.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: A large number of houses were burned down. With regard to whose houses they were, as I said, it is of no importance. Some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you don't know, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you the names. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was there a conflict in Sojevo between the KLA and the army?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In Sojevo and the surrounding villages, there have never been any KLA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So neither in Sojevo nor in your village were there ever any KLA forces. Is that what you're saying? In Kamena Glava or anywhere else in that area?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In our part of this area, that is in our village, there have never been KLA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were there any in Gornje Nerodimje?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Nerodimje and other villages are very far away from my own village, therefore, I can't give you any answers to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these are villages in the same municipality. It's not a big municipality, Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I can speak here about things which I'm completely sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But a short while ago, you said that you did not see any of these things that you are talking about personally.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I said even earlier that I buried the victims. I saw the burning of the houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to go over that. He says he saw the houses burning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You did your military service in 1985/1986; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which service did you serve?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I did my military service in Mali Bor in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but which arms and services?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was -- I did it in the communication, telephone communication service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that on the 8th of April, you saw a tank, M84, and a M60 armoured vehicle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't see only a tank and only an armoured vehicle, M60. There were many -- several tanks and several armoured cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as a signals corps person, how can you know what an M84 is, a tank, and also an armoured vehicle, M60? Where did you acquire this knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I know this. Even a child of 12 or less can say this, can confirm this, because these tanks, these armoured cars, were a daily reality for us Kosovars at that time, from before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But how could you distinguish between the different types of armoured vehicles? You claim that these were the types that you mention in your statement.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But it's easy to distinguish a tank from another armed vehicle which has another shape rather smaller than the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please describe an M84 for us.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: An M84 is a large tank. It has a large calibre cannon with a large barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's the calibre?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this armoured vehicle, M60, what does it have?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Usually they have a large machine-gun which have wreaked havoc among the Albanian population of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, who did you hear say that this was an M60 or an M84, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I am not clear about the question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says that he identified these vehicles himself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't hear that from someone else, that these were the vehicles concerned. You managed to identify them yourself.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I distinguished them myself because, as I said before, armoured vehicles were commonplace in Kosova and had been for a long time, on all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that there is no such thing as an M84, there's only a T84? If we're talking about tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have expert evidence on this in due course. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About tanks? If I saw a photograph, I could tell you that -- I could confirm you which -- confirm for you which tanks were involved in and around my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's not waste any time now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You're challenging this. Let him just identify from the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but he claims that he identified it himself. He claims that he identified it himself, not by having someone show photographs to him. That is what you stated yourself a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can see the photographs that we have here and see if he can identify which it is. Now, if he has 17, he can have a look. Let the witness have a look at Exhibit 17 and see whether he can identify the M60 and the M84.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the armoured vehicle that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just put it on the ELMO and we will see it. Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number 2 in Exhibit 17. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the tank? Yes, we've got that. And the tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the tank that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Number 6 on Exhibit 17. Now, Mr. Milosevic, do you want to ask any questions about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have nothing to ask. He just identified the wrong tank, and you're going to see that because you've marked it with number 6. But let's not waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that -- so the matter is ended, in fairness to the witness, he's identified the BTR60 APC and the T54 or 55 tank. Yes. Thank you. We can put the exhibit back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have seen that he identified the wrong combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will make a judgement about that. I've already said what he did identify, and we've got the pictures. If you think there's a significant difference, so be it. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who jumped out of the APCs and who started running towards your village, did they fire at someone? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw them running to the Cakaj neighbourhood of my village, but they weren't firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, how many people were in the group which was in your column when they left the village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: You mean the number of soldiers or of the civilian population?
