utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the civilians, those who, upon leaving the village, moved in your column. So I mean civilians. How many people were in that group?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were tractors, a lot of tractors in this group. So you cannot tell the total number because, besides the local people, there were also a large number of people from other villages such as Pojatishte Mohovci, Prelez, and many others. And these people had come to Mirosale to seek refuge because, until 8th of April, Mirosale was rather more peaceful than other places and had not been occupied by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, I asked you how many of them were there and you say you can't say how many and there were people from your village and other villages as well. I got that. Now, when you left your village, on the main road you came across a checkpoint set up by the Yugoslav army. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At the exit from Mirosale, following the road to the Gjilan-Ferizaj road or at the entrance to the village of Tankosiq, there was a checkpoint set up by Serbian forces. Adem Berisha, with his Lada car, a red one, was stopped at this checkpoint, and they confiscated his car and forced him to go back. This person was running towards us, and a Serbian soldier fired on him in -- fired in the air, and he came to us, and he climbed into a tractor and continued on the road to Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that two inhabitants of your village started to flee from the soldiers who were at the checkpoint. One was Azem Berisha, whom you've just mentioned. Who was the other one?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Astrit Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were just those two who were in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There were only these two people on the vehicle, and the -- their families were on the trailer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your trailer or in another one nearby, near them?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In the trailer that was in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that the soldiers did not shoot at them, but they shot up in the air. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They fired in the air. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did those two men take cover, then; with you or did they get into the trailer where their families were?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They joined another tractor which they managed to find. It was not important by which trailer they saved themselves, they only wanted to get away from the scene of this tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the occasion, did you pass a checkpoint or did you go back in the direction which you had come from?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Seeing what was happening there, that is on -- that the road to Tankosiq was impassable, we turned and went back in the direction of Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I understood you to say that you had left to go to Sojevo, that you had left that place and went to Sojevo. Is that correct or did I misunderstand you? And I think that's what it says in your statement as well.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: To go to Ferizaj, you have to pass through Sojevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you go to Sojevo when you said that you heard that the army was there? And it was the army and the soldiers that you were escaping from, and it was these people whom you allege had killed seven people in the village of Sojevo and set fire to the houses there.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Well, we went in that direction, putting our dearest ones and ourselves at risk. However, we knew that Serbian forces were there, but your main purpose was for everybody to leave Kosova so that we should never ever go back to Kosova. And so we went in that direction, thinking that even if they killed us, our lives didn't count for much any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were fleeing from that army, from those soldiers, and you claim that they had killed somebody over there. And then you went back to precisely that place where those soldiers were whom, as you said, had killed someone. Is it your explanation that life didn't count for much? Is that why?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Hearing about the various murders, then life becomes cheaper. You can find death anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But why did you flee, then, for the reasons you stated?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We left when the Serbian forces entered my village. So my village was occupied, and it was no longer possible to live there, so we were forced to leave by your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, I understand the explanation you've just given, but would you please answer my questions. So in Sojevo, you came across a military checkpoint as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: If you came across a checkpoint which had narrowed the road, we had to slow down, and a Serbian soldier photographed all the tractors, one by one, and the people in them, and insulted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the soldiers who had previously, according to what you say, in that same village of Sojevo, killed seven people and set fire to the houses, didn't even stop you. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Those who killed in Sojevo, fortunately, because we were a large convoy, did not stop us because they knew very well that this convoy would never return to Kosova but would take the road of no return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you noticed some civilian vehicles there, did you?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It's true. There were civilian vehicles standing in the road, without licence plates or with covered licence plates. There were different civilian trucks prepared for looting, prepared to loot the civilian population of any village they entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And how did you come to that conclusion, passing by their vehicles? How did you know that these were vehicles ready to loot?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I had heard this before from the experience of other different villagers. I knew this from reading newspapers and from other people. And there are also films that I have brought here that document this, and you can see the houses emptied of their contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the inhabitants, didn't they take those things with them when they left?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We couldn't take even the things we needed. We left merely with the clothes on our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you say that, in addition to the soldiers, and you mentioned that there were some paramilitaries there as well, that you just passed by them quite simply. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There on the road, there were military forces. So whether they were paramilitaries or regular units, that's up to you, because they were all uniformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned them, that's why I'm asking you. But let's leave that aside for the moment. You just went past them and nobody harmed you at all. Nobody did anything to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Fortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you crossed the border, nobody took away your ID papers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: On the road from Ferizaj to Han i Elezit, on the road, I saw all sorts of things. And a police entered the bus in Han i Elezit, demanded our documents, identity cards. I was in the back of the bus and, while he was asking for the documents of the other travellers, because the bus was absolutely crammed with people, mainly women and children, and I handed over my identity card with them and put them -- put mine at the bottom of the pile. And I -- he -- I handed it over to the police, and he began to go through them. He identified three or four identity cards and then gave them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he gave everything back to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Returned them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now tell me this: How long have you been a member of the KLA -- of the DSK? I beg your pardon, of the DSK -- LDK.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have been a member of the LDK since the early days, since its formation. And most of the population of Kosova were members of the LDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what about you? Since when have you been a member? Can you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I've been a member of the LDK since 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you have a party function in the LDK at all?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was a member of the Presidency of the LDK in my village, and I was given the job of helping the population with food, because they were constantly under threat of hunger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And the president of your party, in his testimony, says that a large number of the LDK members at the local level were members of the KLA as well. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Regarding what the chairman said, in some other areas where the war had already assumed larger dimensions, this may well have happened and indeed did. But in my village and the other villages around, there were no members of the KLA. I can say that in my village, the members of the Presidency were not members of the KLA but were involved in this time with providing accommodation for the people and helping them with food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And who put you in charge of the refugees, taking care of them?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The members of the village Presidency entrusted me with this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you make lists of refugees and the places they had come from?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Before 24th of March, because the flow of refugees was rather smaller, we compiled a -- certain lists. But later, the flow became much larger and then it was no longer possible to check and list them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many were there before the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Also there was somebody else entrusted with making lists of them at that time, but I was involved in providing them with food then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But I'm not asking you for their names. You said there were not many of them, but how many of them were there? Because in order to provide them with food, you had to know how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: To give them food under regular time, you can give them food such as they like. But under war conditions, bread and salt is enough. So there was no need for any professional preparation of what they were to receive. And their number was around 1.000 to 1.500 people. This is before the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And how many members of the LDK at that time? How many were there?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In Mirosale, there were about 200 members of the LDK. This is related to the period before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why were you afraid then that the police would arrest you if they learnt you were a member of the LDK when there were 200 people in the LDK in your village alone?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Because I was a member of the Presidency, and for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the police arrest any member of the LDK, of you 200?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Some were maltreated, but none were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And was anybody killed on that 6th, 7th, and 8th of April, 1999, in your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Fortunately, no, no one was killed from the village. But a passerby was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what happened to that five-member Serbian family, the only family, in fact, that lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Serb family which remained there up to the 8th of April that we saw it, and then they remained alone, we behaved very well towards this family, all the villagers. And they, too, also behaved in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you happen to know of the crimes of the KLA in your municipality of Urosevac between 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I said we didn't have any KLA in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the Urosevac municipality there was no KLA? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not argue about names. That's the witness's evidence, that there was no KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about some other events that occurred, for example, of the 20th of December, 1998, when a group of KLA members on that day - in the evening, rather - kidnapped Joha Ramadani and his wife Mevluda, Muslia Benush [phoen] and his wife Matim Matesh Afrim [phoen] and Muhajevi Naser [phoen]? This took place in the village of Dramjak. Did you hear about that happening?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I have not heard of this event. This is the first time for me to hear that, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about another event in the village of Doganjevo when they threw hand grenades and shot from automatic rifles at a cafe belonging to Jashar Sarafari, also an Albanian from the village Doganjevo?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: There isn't any such village called Doganjevo in Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us with any actions of the KLA as alleged in Ferizaj, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if there were any KLA presence in Ferizaj, I can assure you that the victims would be in unprecedented numbers. But people in uniforms, KLA uniform, there have never been. Therefore, fortunately, our municipality suffered less casualties compared to other municipalities where there were KLA forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we must -- we must bring this cross-examination to a close in the next minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So where there was no KLA, there were less casualties; is that right? That's what you said a moment ago; right?

utterances.speaker: FLORIM KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In all the areas of Kosova where there was no KLA, the number of victims was smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. We have exhausted our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have nothing to ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No. No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank you and to convey the heartfelt greetings of the families of the victims and especially their mothers who send you their regards. You and all your people who are in Kosova and are rendering great contribution for justice to triumph in Kosova, justice which was in oblivion for several years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must bring that to a close. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand there were some listing difficulties you would like me to address. I'll be very brief because I know time is pressing and I would like to return, perhaps in a private session, to one of the topics we were discussing this morning, for a minute. We have an updated list in the form of a letter to Mr. Dubuisson which I can now distribute. While that's being made available, the problems we face in producing witnesses include that witnesses whose evidence is being given by 92 -- the provisions of 92 bis come in batches. It's only possible to have two batches a week, and we can only roughly get enough witnesses through the Victims and Witnesses Unit, with their great assistance, to fill about two and a half days per week at the average rate we're proceeding at the moment. So that's the underlying or the background problem. As to the particular problem with the witness identified by the accused - we needn't give any names or so on, identifying marks for the moment - for this Thursday, there was another witness who was originally of a similar type coming in for this Thursday. That witness's travel arrangements were compromised by security issues and so that witness couldn't come. Because we can only have about two and a half days of 92 bis witnesses in a week, it's not possible to get more at this rate, another witness had to be brought forward and the decision was made to bring forward the witness about whom the accused spoke this morning and who now features on the latest letter at number 9. So that explains the problem. We're always unhappy when it happens, but our prime concern is to make maximum use of the court time available and there was no other way we could fill it apart from bringing a different category of witness from a 92 bis witness in respect of whom we used our maximum allocation. So that explains at that problem. We do everything we can to avoid these problems occurring, but frequently there are events entirely outside our control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think that, of course, is understood, but it does present the accused and the Chamber with preparation difficulties. So we would be grateful if it's kept to a complete minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I make one other public announcement and then have a minute in private session, if you would allow that. The public announcement is that, by oversight, Exhibit 132 included some pages which are irrelevant. I'll just give you the numbers of the pages. They are serial numbers 00461197 to 1222. They don't relate to that document, they're another document. It's one of the constitutional documents and another constitution crept in by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the constitution of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and another one's crept in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which got in by mistake but no doubt it will be relevant at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be. May we very briefly go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.,
